html:
In 311 CE the armies of the Han Zhao state, founded by Xiongnu leaders, captured and sacked Luoyang, capital of the Jin dynasty. They massacred tens of thousands and took the emperor prisoner. The disaster, named after the Yongjia era, set off a great flight of northern Chinese to the south.

The Western Jin collapsed in 316. North China broke up into the Sixteen Kingdoms, many ruled by peoples from the steppe and frontier. A Jin prince set up a new court at Jiankang, today's Nanjing, founding the Eastern Jin.

Noble families, officials, scholars and many ordinary farmers moved south of the Yangtze. Chinese historians call it "the move south of robes and caps", meaning the old elite. The migrants cleared new land, and the south, until then a frontier, began to grow into the economic heart of China. Over the following centuries the Yangtze valley overtook the north in people and wealth, a shift that the Han census could only hint at.
